summary: This informational memo discusses the problem of securing real-time multimedia sessions. It explains why RTP and RTCP do not mandate a single media security mechanism, which matters to designers and reviewers of RTP extensions.

eli5.summary: There is no single best lock for every type of door. This explains why audio and video streams allow many kinds of locks.

questions: why rtp has no mandatory security
why does rtp not mandate srtp
subtitle: Why RTP leaves media security to a menu of building blocks instead of mandating one solution.

tldr.problem: IETF policy asks every protocol to have a strong, mandatory-to-implement security solution, but RTP is a framework used in very different settings, from phone calls to large multicast streams.
tldr.mechanism: The memo argues that no single media security or key management mechanism fits all RTP uses, so security is chosen as building blocks for each class of application, and payload formats and profiles are not generally the place to mandate it.
tldr.outcome: Specifications for each interoperable class of RTP application must pick their own mandatory-to-implement security, and new payload formats and profiles should reference this memo when they do not.

facts.label: Payload formats at time of writing

today: RFC 7202 is an Informational IETF-stream memo and has not been obsoleted or updated. Its guidance is that security is specified per class of RTP application, with options surveyed in RFC 7201.

sections.title: The Problem with One Security Mechanism
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3550) is widely used for voice over IP, Internet television, video conferencing and other real-time and streaming media. The basic RTP specification offers only limited options for media security and defines no standard key exchange mechanism. Extensions provide confidentiality and authentication of RTP and RTCP, and other mechanisms handle key exchange.

IETF policy in RFC 3365, the so-called Danvers Doctrine, says protocols MUST implement strong security. This memo explains why meeting that requirement does not mean mandating one mechanism for all of RTP. It gives high-level guidance and does not tell an individual implementer which mechanism to choose. A non-exhaustive list of options is in RFC 7201.
sections.eli5: The rule says every protocol needs strong protection. This document explains why RTP cannot just pick one lock for everything.

sections.title: How Widely RTP Is Used
sections.content:
RTP is used in point-to-point voice telephony, video conferencing and telepresence, centralized group conferencing through a Multipoint Conference Unit, Any Source Multicast conferencing, point-to-point streaming, Source-Specific Multicast streaming such as IPTV, replicated unicast streaming, music production and video editing studios, distributed simulation, and streaming real-time sensor data such as e-VLBI radio astronomy.

These range from point-to-point sessions to very large multicast groups, from interactive to non-interactive, and from kilobits per second to multiple gigabits per second. Most run over UDP, but some use TCP or DCCP. Some stay inside one trust domain; others run across domains with untrusted users.
sections.eli5: RTP carries phone calls, TV, music studios and science data. A lock that is right for a private phone call may be wrong for a TV broadcast to millions.

sections.title: Media Security and Key Management
sections.content:
The most widely applicable option is Secure RTP (SRTP, RFC 3711). It is an application-level solution that encrypts the media payload (but not the RTP headers) and optionally supports source origin authentication. It was designed for low overhead, including on links using RTP header compression.

SRTP is not the only choice and does not meet every requirement. For example, ISMACryp payload-level confidentiality suits some streaming video but not voice telephony. The RFC states that no media security protocol is appropriate for every environment where RTP is used, and that several are expected to stay in wide use.

Session establishment and key exchange are likewise diverse. Mechanisms are either in band on the media path or out of band within the session signaling channel. RFC 5479 surveys requirements, and the memo concludes no single key management protocol suits all scenarios.
sections.eli5: SRTP scrambles the sound or picture inside the packet while leaving the address label readable. It works well for many jobs but not for all of them, and there are also different ways to hand out the secret keys.

sections.title: Strong Security in Framework Protocols
sections.content:
The IETF requires a strong, mandatory-to-implement (MTI) security solution so that all implementations of a protocol can interoperate securely. Framework protocols make this hard because they serve different classes of application with different security needs, and implementations for different environments are generally not expected to interwork.

The authors know of no single media security and key management solution that fits the whole range of RTP scenarios and think it unlikely one will appear. Their conclusion is that a framework protocol should offer building blocks for confidentiality, integrity protection, authorization and authentication. When a new use appears, it must be checked against the existing blocks. To maximize interoperability, common mechanisms should be defined for classes of application with similar needs.
sections.eli5: When a rule says everyone must use strong protection but the jobs are very different, the answer is a box of parts. Each kind of job then builds the protection it needs from the same parts.

sections.title: Where Security Is Mandated in RTP
sections.content:
Documents that define an interoperable class of applications using RTP are subject to RFC 3365 and need to specify MTI security. The memo gives WebRTC Security Architecture and RTSP 2.0 as examples under development, and expects a similar document for voice over IP using SIP and RTP.

RTP payload formats describe how a codec's output is carried and can be used by many classes of application, so they are neither secure in themselves nor subject to RFC 3365. They should discuss security implications, should not mandate SRTP, and future ones need to say this and reference this memo. At the time of writing, over 70 payload formats were defined.

RTP profiles are larger extensions. Some may sensibly mandate security building blocks, as RTP/SAVP does. Others, such as RTP/AVPF, apply too widely to do so. A new profile must discuss whether to mandate security, and one that does not specify an interoperable usage must say so with justification and reference this memo.
sections.eli5: If you build a complete game with rules, you must say which lock it uses. If you only build one piece that goes into many games, you should not force a lock on all of them.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
Neither SRTP nor any other single media security solution or keying mechanism can be mandated for all uses of RTP. Each class of application needs its security requirements analyzed, followed by selection of MTI building blocks for traffic protection and key management. The memo expects each class to be covered by a document stating which options are mandatory for that usage scenario.

Its Security Considerations section is one line: the entire memo is about mandatory-to-implement security.
sections.eli5: There is no one-size-fits-all lock for RTP. Each kind of use should say which locks it requires.
